p42.keywords: Nutrition, Chronic wounds, Diabetic foot ulcer, Micronutrient

p: The role of nutrition in wound healing has been the subject of extensive research. Patients with chronic wounds are especially vulnerable to nutrient and micronutrient deficiencies due to the increased nutritional demands of their nonhealing tissues. Despite the increasing literature focusing on specific nutrients and their effects on wound healing, there is a notable lack of large-scale studies that assess the prevalence of micronutrient deficiencies across a wide-ranging chronic wound population.

We conducted a retrospective review on patients evaluated for chronic wounds with varied etiologies such as diabetic foot ulcers, pressure ulcers, post-operative wounds etc. from August 2024 to May 2026 at Mayo Clinic Florida. Micronutrient panels were obtained for zinc, magnesium, iron, ferritin, copper, folate, ceruloplasmin, ascorbic acid, vitamin D, selenium, vitamin A, vitamin B12, vitamin K, vitamin E, and pyridoxal-5-phosphate (vitamin B6) under the guidance of a physician nutritionist. Mean values and the proportion of patients meeting laboratory criteria for deficiency were calculated.

Our cohorts median age was 64 years old (IQR 56,76), with 53% male (n=181) and 47% female patients (n=162), overall, predominantly Caucasian (89%). Magnesium deficiency was the most prevalent finding, present in 133 of 344 patients (38.7%), followed by iron deficiency in 104 patients (30.2%). Vitamin D deficiency was identified in 49 patients (14.2%) and zinc deficiency in 39 patients (11.3%). Ascorbic acid and selenium deficiencies were each present in approximately 8% of the cohort (27/344, 7.8%, and 26/344, 7.6%, respectively). Vitamin B12 deficiency was identified in 15 patients (4.4%). Deficiencies in ferritin, copper, folate, ceruloplasmin, vitamin A, vitamin K, vitamin E, and vitamin B6 were each identified in 7 or fewer patients (≤2.0%).

In our study, magnesium and iron deficiencies were found to be highly prevalent, and a significant number of patients had deficiencies in vitamin D, zinc, vitamin C, and selenium; micronutrients with established roles in wound healing. These findings suggest that micronutrient deficiencies are common in this population and support consideration of routine micronutrient screening as part of chronic wound evaluation with repletion and ongoing surveillance. Further research is needed to determine whether identifying and correcting these deficiencies improves healing outcomes.

p43.keywords: Hidradenitis Suppurativa, minimally invasive therapy, Chronic disease, Outcomes research, Quality of Life

p: Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS) is a chronic, inflammatory skin condition affecting nearly 81 million people that is notorious for significant pain, tunneling, scarring, malodorous discharge adversely affecting the patients’ work, social and sexual life. Due to its recurrence and refractory nature to medical treatment, radical excisions that leave large skin defects are the final resort. We present our experience with using a hydro-surgical minimally invasive treatment as a maintenance therapy in this condition.

MITHS involves debridement of the tunnels with VersajetTM hydro-surgical tool supplemented with laser ablation, botox and steroid injections as needed. We retrospectively analyzed the effectiveness of this therapy in all patients that received it in the time frame ranging from 18 months ago to 1 month ago. The subjective effectiveness was recorded via a verbal questionnaire answered by the patients on a phone call.

A total of 51 patients received the minimally invasive therapy of which 33 (4 with Hurley’s Stage II and 29 with Hurley’s Stage III) patients answered the questionnaire. The average age of the cohort was 37.96 with majority having symptoms starting in the first two decades of life, the average number of years between symptom onset and diagnosis was 6.12 years. The average pain score before the procedure was 6.21 which was reduced to 3.13 after the procedure, with patients reporting an average of 73% resolution of symptoms and average remission period of 74 days.

Surgical excision which is the gold standard for management of HS often results in massive open wounds requiring weeks of extensive wound care, necessitating admission to wound care facilities or deployment of home health services and could still recur. This treatment protocol supplemented with medical management will help downstage Hidradenitis Suppurativa, resulting in longer remission periods, reduced frequency and severity of symptoms, improved quality of life, preventing radical excision and need for reconstructive surgeries. We found this technique to be non-inferior compared to deroofing as it excises the tunnels, followed by scarring leading to decrease in overlying sebaceous gland and hair follicle growth.

p: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is frequently diagnosed at an advanced stage despite prior imaging examinations. We evaluated whether blinded review of prior low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) examinations identified pancreatic abnormalities more frequently in patients who subsequently developed PDAC than in matched controls.

We performed a retrospective descriptive study including 13 patients who subsequently developed PDAC and 52 comparison patients selected for similar age and sex. A board-certified radiologist, blinded to clinical outcomes, independently reviewed all prior low-dose chest computed tomography (LDCT) examinations using the RADPEER scoring system while documenting predefined pancreatic imaging findings. Continuous variables were compared using Student's t-test or the Mann-Whitney U test, as appropriate, and categorical variables using Fisher's exact test.

Sixty-five patients (13 PDAC cases and 52 comparison patients) were included. Cases and comparison patients were similar in age and sex. The median interval from prior LDCT to PDAC diagnosis was 10 months (IQR, 6–26). Most PDACs arose in the pancreatic head (46%), and 70% of staged patients had stage IV disease at diagnosis. Blinded review of all 65 examinations classified the pancreas as normal in 69%, insufficiently visualized in 5%, and abnormal in 26%. Among evaluable examinations, RADPEER discrepancies (score ≥2) were more frequent in PDAC cases than the comparison group (50% vs. 2%, p = 0.0001). Abnormal pancreatic findings were also more common in cases (58% vs. 20%, p = 0.013), including pancreatic masses (25% vs. 0%, p = 0.006) and common bile duct dilation (17% vs. 0%, p = 0.035).

Blinded review of prior LDCT examinations using RADPEER criteria identified significantly more interpretive discrepancies and pancreatic abnormalities in patients who subsequently developed PDAC than in the comparison group. These findings suggest that pancreatic abnormalities may be retrospectively identifiable on chest LDCT before PDAC diagnosis.

p49.keywords: Acute pain, Multimodal Analgesia, sodium channel blockers, non-opioid medication, postsurgical pain

p: Suzetrigine is a first-in-class, non-opioid oral analgesic that selectively blocks NaV1.8 voltage-gated sodium channels and was approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in January 2025 for moderate-to-severe acute pain in adults. Early prescribing patterns remain poorly described.
To evaluate early inpatient and outpatient suzetrigine prescribing patterns at a large academic medical center.

We performed a retrospective chart review of all patients prescribed suzetrigine at Mayo Clinic from April-December 2025. Demographic and clinical characteristics, prescribing department, dosing regimen, multimodal analgesia (MMA) co-prescribing, refill patterns, and adverse events were analyzed separately for inpatient and outpatient groups. MMA was defined as suzetrigine prescribed with at least 2 additional analgesics of different mechanisms within the same encounter. Continuous variables were compared using Mann-Whitney U tests and categorical variables using Pearson chi-square tests; p<0.05 was significant.

A total of 1,280 prescriptions were reviewed (821 inpatient, 458 outpatient). Multimodal analgesia co-prescribing was more common inpatient, including opioids, acetaminophen, gabapentin, ketamine, and local anesthetics (all p<0.001), whereas NSAID use was slightly higher in outpatient population (p=0.048). Colorectal surgery was the most frequent inpatient prescriber, while otorhinolaryngology led outpatient use. FDA-labeled loading doses were more common inpatient, while outpatient prescriptions often omitted loading. Indications differed by setting (inpatient: predominantly acute surgical pain; outpatient: mixed acute surgical and chronic pain; p<0.001). Refills were rare inpatient, but occurred regularly in outpatient. Adverse events were uncommon (2.9%) and did not differ by care setting.

Early suzetrigine prescribing differed between inpatient and outpatient settings in specialty use, MMA co-prescribing, dosing, indication, and refill patterns. These data provide an early benchmark for clinical integration.

p51.keywords: Odontoidectomy, Endoscopic Endonasal approach, Transoral approach, basillar invagination

p: Irreducible ventral compression of the craniovertebral junction typically requires anterior decompression via odontoidectomy often with posterior stabilization. The transoral approach (TOA) has long been the standard, but the endoscopic endonasal approach (EEA) has more recently emerged as a less invasive alternative. We combined an institutional cohort with a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing perioperative and neurological outcomes between approaches.

We performed a retrospective cohort study of odontoidectomy with posterior stabilization at the 3 Mayo Clinic sites, combined with a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing baseline, operative, and postoperative variables. Pooled proportions were analyzed by approach using logit-transformed data and generalized linear mixed models, with subgroup comparisons and direct pairwise meta-analysis.

The institutional cohort comprised 36 patients (10 EEA, 26 TOA). EEA patients were younger (p=0.023) and had higher rates of diabetes (p=0.039) and sleep apnea (p=0.010), while preoperative sensory deficit was more common in the transoral group (p=0.011). Complete odontoidectomy was achieved in 32 patients. Patient undergoing EEA had more posterior levels fused and had greater blood loss.

The meta-analysis included 23 unique studies comprising 549 patients including our cohort. Pooled neurological improvement was 95.5% for EEA and 91.1% for TOA, and adequate decompression was 99.2% and 98.4%, respectively. CSF leak was more frequent after EEA (6.3% vs 1.5%), while dysphagia was more frequent after TOA (12.0% vs 0.8%). Heterogeneity was low-to-moderate for neurological improvement (I²=29.9%) and moderate for transoral dysphagia (I²=48.4%) in the TOA group. Subgroup differences were non-significant for all outcomes, though CSF leak approached significance (Q=3.46, p=0.063). Pairwise meta-analysis, feasible only for neurological improvement and CSF leak, suggested lower odds of neurological improvement with endonasal surgery (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.42–0.78) based on only two informative studies, and an imprecise CSF leak estimate (OR 2.64, 95% CI 0.02–328)

EEA and TOA odontoidectomy showed similar rates of decompression and neurological improvement, with no significant differences between approaches. The observed differences were mainly associated with corridor-specific morbidity. These findings may reflect a role for anatomy and comorbidity in corridor selection.

p57.keywords: Alzheimer's Disease, expansion microscopy, astrocytes, extracellular vesicles, high-resolution imaging

p: Astrocyte-mediated intercellular communication, including interactions at tripartite synapses and extracellular vesicle (EV)-mediated signaling, may contribute to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathogenesis. However, the nanoscale structures underlying these processes remain difficult to resolve in situ by conventional fluorescence microscopy due to the diffraction limit of light.

An AAV vector carrying HA-TurboID-hCD9 under the astrocyte-specific GFAP promoter was injected into the hippocampal dentate gyrus of 3-month-old mice, whose brains were collected, fixed, and sectioned three weeks post-injection. These fixed sections then underwent expansion microscopy (ExM), which embeds tissue in a swell-able polymer and isotropically enlarges it, effectively increasing its spatial resolution. Expanded sections were then acquired as single-plane and z-stack confocal images, focusing on regions of interest including synaptic regions immunolabeled for VGLUT1 and Homer-1 as pre- and postsynaptic markers, and HA-CD9-positive structures representing astrocytic membranes. Three-dimensional Imaris reconstructions were generated to better examine their special relationships within surrounding neuronal architecture.

ExM achieved a 7-8x tissue expansion, corresponding to an effective lateral resolution of around 25-30 nm compared with ~200 nm using conventional fluorescence microscopy, allowing for the visualization of EV-sized structures (~50–150 nm). Fine astrocytic processes and TurboID-CD9-positive structures could be visualized as structures with defined shapes and volumes rather than point-like signals, facilitating assessment of their three-dimensional spatial relationships within surrounding neuronal architecture. ExM improved the spatial resolution of VGLUT1 and Homer-1 labeling, allowing pre- and postsynaptic structures to be clearly resolved in close apposition. Spherical HA–TurboID–CD9-positive structures consistent with EV-like morphology were resolved in neuronal structures, including signals localized beyond clearly identifiable astrocytic processes.

ExM enables high-resolution, three-dimensional visualization of fine astrocytic and HA-positive structures in brain tissue using conventional fluorescence microscopy without specialized equipment. Combined with astrocyte-selective TurboID-CD9 labeling, this approach provides a framework for investigating the distribution and fate of astrocyte-derived EVs in the brain.

p: Glomus tumors are benign mesenchymal tumors composed of modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body. Acral glomus tumors are commonly found in the upper extremities, specifically in the subungual area of the digits. Upper extremity nonacral glomus tumors are considerably less common and remain inadequately explored in the literature. The aim of this study was to further characterize and compare the clinical presentation and treatment outcomes for upper extremity acral and nonacral glomus tumors.

A retrospective review was performed on patients diagnosed with upper extremity glomus tumors across multiple tertiary referral centers from 1994-2026. Patients were categorized as having acral or nonacral tumors. Primary outcomes of interest included demographic variables, tumor size, tumor location, treatment pathways, and history of recurrence.

A total of 159 patients were identified, including 98 acral (61.6%) and 61 nonacral (38.4%). Acral tumors were more common in women (65.3%), whereas nonacral tumors predominated in men (82.0%; p,0.001). Acral lesions most frequently involved the ring finger (25.5%), middle finger (20.4%), and thumb (16.3%) while nonacral tumors were most common in the forearm (44.3%), arm (19.7%), and elbow (16.4%) (all p<0.001). Surgical excision was performed in 90.8% of acral and 65.6% of nonacral cases, with recurrence rates of 15.7% and 32.5%, respectively (p=0.038).

This study represents one of the largest analyses of acral and nonacral upper extremity glomus tumors. Acral tumors are more likely to be found in patients with a history of neurofibromatosis, while nonacral tumors were significantly more common in males. While age at diagnosis was similar between groups, recurrence rates following surgical excision were significantly higher in nonacral tumors.

p: Early readmission after pancreatic resection remains a significant challenge. We sought to identify predictors of 30-day surgical readmission and assess their consistency across pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) and distal pancreatectomy (DP).

We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of pancreatic resections performed between 2018 and 2024. The primary outcome was unplanned 30-day surgical readmission; secondary outcomes included any readmission and index-admission reoperation. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors, with Firth penalization applied to procedure-specific models.

Among 636 patients, 127 (20.0%) experienced surgical readmission. In multivariable analysis, ASA class IV (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 8.51, 95% CI 2.27–31.59), postoperative pancreatic fistula (aOR 5.59, 95% CI 2.72–11.53), delayed gastric emptying (aOR 6.24, 95% CI 3.32–11.77), and abdominal abscess (aOR 15.21, 95% CI 7.52–32.32) independently predicted surgical readmission. Pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying, and abdominal abscess remained significant in both PD and DP subgroups, without significant interactions by procedure type. Any 30-day readmission occurred in 149 of 653 patients (22.8%). An exploratory complication-based risk stratification demonstrated increasing surgical readmission rates from 7.4% without complications to 90.9% with all three complications (p for trend <0.001).

Pancreas-specific complications and poor preoperative physiologic status are strongly associated with early surgical readmission, with consistent findings across PD and DP. Identifying these complications before discharge may help guide risk-adapted postoperative surveillance and discharge planning.

p: Traditional postoperative metrics inadequately capture the complexity of pancreatic surgery, prompting adoption of the composite Textbook Outcome (TBO) as a more comprehensive benchmark. We evaluated the impact of surgical approach on TBO after pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) or distal pancreatectomy (DP).

We performed a single-center retrospective study of all PD-DP resections performed at Mayo Clinic Florida between 2010–2024, excluding total pancreatectomy, unclassified resections, and conversions. The primary outcome, TBO, defined as absence of clinically relevant pancreatic fistula, postpancreatectomy hemorrhage, major complications, 30-day readmission, and in-hospital mortality. Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of TBO failure, stratified by procedure type. Results are reported as adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals.

Among 1,218 resections (718 PD; 500 DP), TBO was achieved in 67.0% of PD and 84.8% of DP. In PD, TBO failure (33.0%) did not differ significantly by surgical approach (p=0.103). Liver fibrosis or cirrhosis (aOR 3.96, 95% CI 1.20–13.10; p=0.024) and vascular resection (aOR 1.69, 95% CI 1.02–2.82; p=0.044) independently predicted TBO failure, whereas pancreatic or periampullary adenocarcinoma was associated with lower odds (aOR 0.60, 95% CI 0.41–0.88; p=0.009). In DP, TBO failure occurred in 15.2% and differed significantly by approach (30.4% open, 11.6% laparoscopic, 25.7% robotic; p<0.001). Laparoscopic DP was independently associated with lower odds of TBO failure compared with open resection (aOR 0.31, 95% CI 0.16–0.61; p<0.001). Age was not independently associated with TBO failure in either cohort.
Our findings highlight that surgical approach influences TBO in DP but not pancreaticoduodenectomy, with laparoscopic DP achieving the highest composite outcomes and age alone not limiting success.
